finding.title: Device agent.resume releases workstation-approved shell sessions held by the pause gate
finding.scenario: A Mission approved by the workstation (envelope authority workstation) has a Claude write step (Bash/PowerShell allowed). While the owning Agent is paused, missionPauseGate holds the step: zero sessions start. A paired device holds the 'supervise' right for agent.resume (device-authority.server.ts:64). resume() (agent-runtime.server.ts:196-240) has no device-specific check beyond the revision, then calls missions.schedule() (line 239). tickOnce -> launch -> approveDelegated starts the held Claude shell session with no device approval, no trusted-desktop grant and no pending request. The device therefore chooses when workstation-held code execution begins, which the Host's own deviceStartRefusal (manager.server.ts:2076-2086) and round-1 fix (6) say a device must never do for mission.start.
finding.evidence: Probe (throwaway mkdtemp, MissionManager + TaskManager, fake claude adapter): approve(workstation, start=true) with missionPauseGate=()=>true -> launched=0, mission state running. Then missionPauseGate=()=>false and schedule(id) -> launched=1 provider=claude access=write allowedTools='Read,Write,Edit,Bash,PowerShell', authority={kind:'workstation'}, requests=0. Gate read at manager.server.ts:873 and declared at :82; wired at http.server.ts:296; device right at device-authority.server.ts:64. The device route through agent-runtime resume was traced in code, not exercised end-to-end (no AgentRuntime harness).
finding.recommendation: Apply the same rule to device agent.resume that deviceStartRefusal applies to mission.start: refuse a device resume (or the schedule it triggers) when any step that would be admitted under a workstation envelope can start a shell-capable session, terminal or hook-running Git. Alternatively, make launch-time device-triggered starts re-run deviceStartRefusal-equivalent checks.

Not refuted. The mechanism is confirmed by code reading; I did not rerun the probe.

Mechanism, each link checked:
- agent-runtime.server.ts:196-240 (resume): the only device-specific check is the consent revision (line 210-211). It clears the pause (saveProfile pausedAt null, flags paused false, line 230-231), then calls this.missions.schedule(agent.missionId!) at line 239.
- agent-runtime.server.ts:74-78 (blockedForMission) reads the durable paused flag, so once resume clears it the gate returns false.
- manager.server.ts:862-873 (tickOnce): a paused mission admits no new step; after the gate lifts, the ready step goes through launch and approveDelegated (manager.server.ts:996-1026). The launch path has no actor check, and a workstation envelope needs no desktop grant.
- device-authority.server.ts:64 grants "agent.resume" the "supervise" right, so a device can reach this path.
- The 15s supervised loop (manager.server.ts:297) also reschedules running missions, so any resume leads to admission within about 15s.
- deviceStartRefusal (manager.server.ts:2076-2086) is enforced only for mission.start (commands.server.ts:60). Agent missions cannot be started remotely at all (commands.server.ts:55), so the device's only route to a shell-capable admission is resume.

Scope of harm: the workstation approved the envelope with start, so the device does not add authority. The concrete issue is that a device can undo a workstation-issued pause and start shell-capable sessions at a time the device picks. That is exactly the principle the Host's own comment at manager.server.ts:2073-2075 says a device must never do for mission.start. Resume is a granted device right, so this is an inconsistency with the stated principle rather than a clear policy violation. Hence MEDIUM, not BLOCKER. Counterpoint I checked: a device can only lift a hold, not start a mission that is not already running, so it cannot begin execution from a non-started state.

No repo files were edited. I did not run any test or probe; my verification was static reading of the code paths listed above.

Not refuted; the claimed path is real by code reading, and I did not run a new probe (the claimant's MissionManager probe was not re-run).

Preconditions checked:
- Device resume is reachable. DEVICE_RIGHTS maps "agent.resume" to "supervise" (device-authority.server.ts:64). agentCommand dispatches it unconditionally for devices (agent-runtime.server.ts:925-929). The only device block in agentCommand is agent.create and agent.start (agent-runtime.server.ts:868-869), so a device cannot start an Agent but can resume one.
- resume() (agent-runtime.server.ts:196-240) has no device-specific refusal beyond the consent revision check at :213. It has no equivalent of deviceStartRefusal. It clears the pause, then calls missions.schedule(agent.missionId) at :239.
- The pause gate holds steps only while paused. missionPauseGate is read at manager.server.ts:873 and blockedForMission (agent-runtime.server.ts:74-78) reads the paused flag. Clearing the flag lets tickOnce admit the held ready steps.
- Contrast: commands.server.ts:60 refuses a device mission.start when deviceStartRefusal (manager.server.ts:2076-2086) is non-null. That refusal covers exactly the shell/terminal/hook-Git envelope case. The same envelope can therefore be started by a device through agent.resume but not through mission.start.
- Pause records no actor. The pause path saves only pausedAt plus paused:true (agent-runtime.server.ts ~:180-185), and resume does not check who paused. So a workstation-set pause, which is a deliberate hold on code execution, can be lifted by a paired device.

Why not higher than MEDIUM: resume releases only steps already admitted under a workstation-approved envelope. It grants no new authority, does not create requests, and does not change the envelope. The device controls timing and can override a workstation hold, but it cannot cause execution outside the workstation-approved scope. The policy text ("pause/resume/stop within authority") is ambiguous on whether resume counts as authorization.

Recommendation stands: refuse device agent.resume when the mission's envelope would admit shell/terminal/hook-Git steps, or at least refuse device lifting of a workstation-recorded pause. Repo files were not touched and no test-results changes resulted.

finding.title: Device allow_once on a provider ask ignores envelope expiry and session/budget limits at launch
finding.scenario: Workstation Mission with a tool-free Ollama read step. Dispatch correctly refuses the launch (taskViolation: expiry, provider-session budget, external budget, roots) and raises a provider.execute ask. deviceRequestRefusal (manager.server.ts ~1990-2000) only checks deviceMayLaunch, which passes for local Ollama, so a device can answer allow_once. respondMission -> tasks.approve -> launch -> missionScopeCheck, which calls providerScopeViolation and never re-checks expiresAt, sessionsUsed/maxSessions or the external-call budget that taskViolation enforces at dispatch. The Ollama session therefore launches outside the envelope's time and budget limits.
finding.evidence: Probe: (a) envelope.expiresAt set to the past -> ask reason 'ollama for Summarize: authorization expired'; device mission.respond allow_once accepted; launchedAfterDeviceAllow=1, sessionAuthority tool_free. (b) providers.sessions.maxSessions=0 -> reason 'provider-session budget exhausted'; device allow_once accepted; session launched. Checks present only in authorization.server.ts:426-440 (taskViolation) and absent from the launch gate at manager.server.ts:94-112; respond path at manager.server.ts:3468 (this.tasks.approve(step.taskId, by)). Impact is limited to tool-free Ollama (no shell, no tools), but a device overrides explicit workstation envelope bounds.
finding.recommendation: Make the launch-time gate (missionScopeCheck 'check'/'launch') enforce the same envelope limits as taskViolation: expiry, revocation, provider-session budget, external-call budget and project roots. Or have respondMission re-run taskViolation before tasks.approve and refuse a device answer when it fails.

votes.reasoning:
The mechanism is real, confirmed by code reading (no probe run, no repo files touched).
- manager.server.ts:94-112 (missionScopeCheck) checks only envelope.revokedAt; it never checks expiresAt, the provider-session budget or the external-call budget. Those live only in authorization.server.ts:426-440 (taskViolation).
- TaskManager.approve (bunny-host/manager.server.ts:974-990) goes straight to launch(), and launch() calls missionScopeCheck (lines 1047 and 1129/1136) without taskViolation. approveDelegated's check callback is not used by the direct approve path.
- agenticProviderCheck (manager.server.ts:2551-2552) returns null when no Agentic record exists, so non-Agentic missions get no expiry or budget check at launch.
- respond() (manager.server.ts ~3355-3470) runs deviceRequestRefusal, which for provider.execute only calls deviceMayLaunch (device-authority.server.ts:33-36, TOOL_FREE_PROVIDERS = {"ollama"}, not remote tag). Nothing in respond re-runs taskViolation before tasks.approve. The finding's probe result is therefore consistent with the code.
Why I rate it LOW rather than MEDIUM:
- The device path is limited to tool-free local Ollama: no shell, no tools, no file writes, no code execution. That is outside the policy's must-never list.
- The same launch happens when the workstation itself answers allow_once to this ask, so this is not a device-specific escalation. It is a consistency gap in the direct-approval path.
- Impact is one child session per answer. Dispatch of later steps still runs taskViolation at manager.server.ts:1388, so the overrun does not repeat.
- The codebase's own intent is visible: respondBatch (~3279) refuses an expired envelope with "approve the mission again", so an answer should not extend expired authority. The gap is real but narrow.
The recommendation (re-run taskViolation before approve or in the launch gate) is sound.

finding.title: Trusted-desktop grant can never start a shell session in an Agent-owned remote Mission
finding.scenario: For a remote Agent Mission, a shell-capable provider session needs a valid trusted-desktop grant. launch() runs missionAttemptAdmission -> admitAgenticProvider, whose validate callback is agenticProviderCheck(task) ?? taskViolation(task, stored envelope, ...) with no desktopGrant option. taskViolation -> providerScopeViolation -> remoteSessionViolation returns a violation for claude write / codex, so admission refuses even when the workstation granted and the grant check passed. Fail-closed (no bypass), but the desktop-approval path is dead for Agent Missions and the approval the user gave cannot take effect.
finding.evidence: Code trace only; not probed (AgentRuntime harness not built). admitAgenticProvider at manager.server.ts:2583; validate lambda with taskViolation at :2605; launch admission call at bunny-host/manager.server.ts ~1133 runs before the 'launch' spend; providerScopeViolation options path at authorization.server.ts:420-421 is not used here.
finding.recommendation: Pass the grant-aware decision into the admission validate (for example via the same desktopGrant option or a shared helper), or make the admission call consume the grant after validation, so approved Agent sessions can start.

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted. The claim holds on code trace plus a pure-function probe.

Code path: an Agent-owned Mission launch runs TaskManager.launch (bunny-host/manager.server.ts ~1129 check, then 1132 missionAttemptAdmission) before the "launch" spend at ~1136. admitAgenticProvider (bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:2583-2612) passes validate = agenticProviderCheck(task) ?? taskViolation(...) with no desktopGrant option. taskViolation calls providerScopeViolation without options (authorization.server.ts:426-440, :420-421), so remoteSessionViolation (:180-186) refuses claude write / codex sessions for any remote envelope. agentic.admit (agentic-store.server.ts:126-131) returns the reason before any ADMITTED row is written, so the launch throws. The grant-aware check in missionScopeCheck (manager.server.ts:94-120) only runs on the Mission path, and admission is skipped for non-agentic missions.

Reachability: a paired device can produce a remote Agent envelope. agent-runtime.server.ts:884-893 routes agent.authorization.approve from a device to reauthorizeAgent(missionId, rev, actor) when the mission is not waiting_for_approval, and deviceAgenticRefusal (manager.server.ts:2025-2040) skips provider.execute. reauthorizeAgent (:2225-2270) then saves envelopeFrom(..., actor) with grantedBy "device:...", which is remote authority with sessionCeiling tool_free/read_tools.

Probe (temp dir, deleted afterwards): a remote device envelope with a claude write step gives remoteSessionViolation = "...claude write sessions run with shell authority.", providerScopeViolation without grant = same refusal, providerScopeViolation with desktopGrant:true = null, and taskViolation (the admission validate path) = same refusal. So the grant cannot satisfy admission for Agent Missions.

Security impact: none found. It is fail-closed, no device can start a shell session, and the grant is never spent on this path. Impact is functional: the owner-approved "request for later trusted-desktop approval" does not take effect for Agent remote write/Codex sessions. The finding's LOW severity is fair. No repo files were edited and no repo tests were run; test-results/ shows no changes.

The reported refusal does occur, but the claimed cause and fix are incomplete. In an Agent-owned Mission, a Claude write or Codex session (and Claude read) is refused by a grant-independent gate before the grant is ever consulted. missionScopeCheck (manager.server.ts:104) calls agenticProviderCheck(task) right after providerScopeViolation, and agenticProviderCheck (manager.server.ts ~2561-2575) returns agenticScopeViolation(e, "provider.execute", ...). agenticScopeViolation (authorization.server.ts ~390) allows provider.execute only for ollama with access "read" and filesystem false. Probe: agenticScopeViolation returns "Workspace provider tools cannot enforce this exact Agent resource/terminal scope" for claude write, codex write and claude read, and null only for ollama read. So passing the grant into the admission validate (the recommendation) would not make an approved Agent shell session start. The grant path is unreachable for Agent Missions by the T5 confinement already documented in devicesAgenticRefusal ("T5 confines Agentic model delegation to tool-free local inference"). This is fail-closed, not a security bypass, and it is consistent with the Agent design, so it is not a LOW correctness defect. At most it is a documentation/UX note (an ask can be raised that can never be honored). Probe folder deleted; repo untouched; no test run beyond none.

finding.title: deviceStartRefusal refuses every workstation Mission with provider execution, including tool-free Ollama only
finding.scenario: shellSessions is true whenever providers.execution is true and writeIncludesShell is not false. writeIncludesShell is hard-set to true for every workstation envelope (authorization.server.ts:81), independent of step access or provider. No code execution is enabled by this; it is a LOW correctness/usability issue. Recommended correction: fold step-level providerConstraints.allow into the candidate set, keeping unknown = shell. finding.title: startSession binds the grant to the stale effort, not the effort actually launched
finding.scenario: startSession builds targetTask = {...current, provider, model} and keeps current.effort, while the persisted and launched record uses target.effort (escalate-effort). missionScopeCheck and sessionOperation therefore compare the grant against the old effort. Not reachable in current flows: every shell session start consumes the single-use grant at its first launch, and a relaunch on the same provider/model cannot obtain a new grant for that Task. Recorded as a binding gap against the stated exact-operation policy.
finding.evidence: Code reading of bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1282 and the escalate-effort branch (~1554-1566); sessionOperation at authorization.server.ts:~370 includes effort.
finding.recommendation: Use {...current, provider: target.provider, model: target.model, effort: target.effort ?? null} for targetTask so the check sees exactly what will launch.

finding.title: Failed approval leaves an unspent desktop grant valid for up to 5 minutes
finding.scenario: respondMission mints the grant (line 3401) and saves the request as resolved before calling tasks.approve (line 3468). If approve throws, the catch calls stepFailed but does not revoke the grant. The grant stays valid, unspent, and bound to that Task for its 5-minute TTL. Only a workstation action could use it again (device approve refuses mission Tasks; respond refuses a non-waiting step), so the impact is hygiene, not a device path.
finding.evidence: Code reading of manager.server.ts:3401-3412 and 3466-3478; revokeDesktopGrants is called only from stop, retry and replan.

finding.title: Trusted-desktop operation digest skips --flag=path script arguments, so an approved script can change before it runs
finding.scenario: The owner approves a terminal.exec such as node --require=./x.cjs scripts/ok.mjs. The grant binds content hashes only for names that do not start with '-', so the --require=./x.cjs value is never hashed. The device then rewrites x.cjs (ordinary write, not refused) before the step runs. At consume time capabilityOperation() still yields the same digest and the same files map, so desktopGrantConsume passes and node loads the device-written code. The control form '-r ./x.cjs' is hashed correctly.
finding.evidence: Probe: capabilityOperation('terminal.exec',{command:'node',args:['--require=./x.cjs','scripts/ok.mjs']},repo,null).files contains only scripts/ok.mjs. After rewriting x.cjs the whole operation JSON is identical (unchanged:true). With args ['-r','./x.cjs','scripts/ok.mjs'] the files map includes ./x.cjs.
finding.recommendation: For each argument that starts with '-', also split at the first '=' and hash the right-hand side when it resolves to an existing file. Simpler: hash every argument that resolves to an existing regular file under cwd, whatever its prefix.

Probe in a mkdtemp folder: capabilityOperation('terminal.exec',{command:'node',args:['--require=./x.cjs','scripts/ok.mjs']}) yields files keys ["./x.cjs","scripts/ok.mjs"]. The finding's "unchanged:true" did not reproduce. (2) After rewriting x.cjs, the operation JSON changes (digest-and-files-equal: false), so sameOperation() rejects it ("The operation differs from the one authorized on the desktop."). (3) Independently, any device filesystem.write admitted after approval is saved as a capability_runs row (bus.server.ts:278 saveRun before execution), and mutationSequence() (store.server.ts:149-151) counts 'filesystem.write'; probe: same operation with mutationSequence 5 -> 6 yields "Project files changed after trusted-desktop authorization". Consume is checked at bus.server.ts ~line 262 (desktopGrantConsume) before saveRun, so the sequence guard works. No other project-writing path bypasses capability_runs (artifacts.server.ts writes to the Host data folder; bounded-terminal snapshot writes to a snapshot directory on the agentic path only; git-merge marker is refused remotely). Residual, distinct and LOW: fileIdentities() does not hash URL-form operands such as --import=file:///<abs>/x.mjs (probe: files = ["scripts/ok.mjs"] only). Node honours that form. Post-approval rewrites are still blocked by mutationSequence, so the practical effect is the accepted pre-approval limitation class, not a device-triggered execution after approval. Also noted, not part of the claim: after desktopGrantConsume spends the grant there is no re-hash before the child process starts, so a write admitted in the consume-to-spawn window would still reach node. This applies to plain named scripts too, is timing-dependent, and was not probed end to end. Probe folder deleted; no repo file written; npm/test not run.

The claimed digest gap is not present in the current code. authorization.server.ts:225 maps "--flag=value" to its right-hand side ("--require=./x.cjs" becomes "./x.cjs"), and fileIdentities() at lines 220-235 hashes it. A probe in a mkdtemp folder under the OS temp dir (deleted afterwards) gave files keys ["./x.cjs","scripts/ok.mjs"] for --require=./x.cjs, and the digest changed after rewriting x.cjs (unchanged:false). The '-r ./x.cjs' form is hashed too. The finding's stated evidence (files contains only scripts/ok.mjs) does not reproduce.

Even where a file is not hashed, the scenario cannot complete. Every device filesystem.write, filesystem.delete, terminal.exec, git commit/merge/worktree and browser.download is saved as a capability_run row before it executes (capabilities/bus.server.ts:278, store.server.ts:149-150). mutationSequence() counts those rows, and desktopGrantViolation (authorization.server.ts:267) voids the grant when the count changes. consumeDesktopGrant recomputes the operation with the current mutationSequence (manager.server.ts:2143, 2160). So a device rewrite of x.cjs after approval is refused at consume time. The only residual is that file: URL specifiers (for example --import=file:///... or --loader file:///...) are not hashed by fileIdentities (probe: files = ["scripts/ok.mjs"] only). This is defence-in-depth only, because the mutation-sequence guard still refuses any device rewrite. It is INFO at most, and I did not classify it as a separate finding. No repo tests were run and no repo files were changed.

finding.title: Remote filesystem writes and deletes ignore Host private state under a broad mission root

The comment at paths.server.ts:28 says private state is never a resource even under a broad root, and this path violates it. finding.title: A grant is spent before the agentic revalidate step, so a failed revalidate burns a single-use approval
finding.scenario: desktopGrantConsume (line 274) spends the single use. The adapter then runs delegated.revalidate() (line 290) and can throw before the adapter executes. The desktop approval is lost and the operation must be approved again. Fail-closed, so it does not expand authority.
finding.evidence: Code order at bus.server.ts:274 (consume) before :290 (revalidate throw). Not probed dynamically.
finding.recommendation: Move the consume to after the last refusal point, or refund the use when revalidate or admission fails before spawn.

finding.title: Possible time-of-check/time-of-use gap between grant hashing and process spawn
finding.scenario: The grant's file hashes are checked in desktopGrantConsume (bus.server.ts:274), then the adapter awaits outputPipe (owned-process-group.server.ts:137) before the owned process spawns. A concurrent device filesystem.write to a hashed script can land in that window, so node may read content the owner did not approve. Code-level window only; not reproduced dynamically.
finding.evidence: Await ordering in runWindowsOwnedProcess before the OwnedProcessGroup spawn; no re-hash after the await.
finding.recommendation: Re-verify the named file identities immediately before spawn, or block remote writes to any file named by an active terminal grant until the process starts.

votes.reasoning:
The gap is real and the claimed mechanism holds. I did not refute it.

Code path, verified by reading:
- bus.server.ts:274-276 runs desktopGrantConsume, which recomputes fileIdentities (authorization.server.ts:220-232) and compares them with the grant via sameOperation. Consume is synchronous and spends the use.
- bus.server.ts:292 awaits found.adapter.execute. local.server.ts:165 calls runProcess, which goes to runWindowsOwnedProcess (process.server.ts:65).
- owned-process-group.server.ts:137 and :140 each await outputPipe (named-pipe listen). Only after those awaits does :142-143 spawn. Node then reads the named script after boot. Nothing re-hashes the named files after consume.
- Nothing blocks a device write in that window. remoteExecutionRefusal (authorization.server.ts:208-212) refuses only executionConfigPath targets (.git, .gitattributes, package.json, etc.). A project .js file is not in that set. Step workspace locks (manager.server.ts:1160/2686) gate step admission only, not bus capability requests. mutationSequence (store.server.ts:149) is compared only at consume, so a write after consume is never detected for this grant.
- The bounded agentic path is different: snapshotBoundedTest (bounded-terminal.server.ts:70-80) copies and hash-checks the script synchronously before launch. The desktop path has no such snapshot. The finding's scope is correct.

Probe (throwaway mkdtemp folder under the OS temp dir, since deleted): a file was hashed as approved, then runWindowsOwnedProcess(node, [script]) was called. A writeFileSync was scheduled with setImmediate, which lands during the pipe-listen await. Output: stdout "INJECTED", exitCode 0, ownership state "succeeded". The owner-approved content was not what ran. The rmSync EPERM at the end was a probe cleanup artifact; the folder was then removed with rm -rf and confirmed gone.

Severity reasoning: the finding's LOW understates it. The round-1 fix was meant to make a terminal grant bind content, and this gap defeats that binding. Under the stated policy a device-triggered write landing in the post-consume window would give unconstrained code execution under a desktop-approved node run. Exploitation is not trivially reproduced at bus level. It needs a device-approvable write to a grant-named file that lands in the window of tens of milliseconds, and it needs a pending write for that file. That keeps it below HIGH, so MEDIUM is my call.

Two further points for the author. First, the recommended re-verify before spawn does not close the gap, because node reads the file after spawn. Only blocking writes to grant-named files until the process starts, or snapshotting as the bounded path does, closes it. Second, imported modules that node loads lazily are not hashed at all, and writes to them after consume are never checked for the whole run. The same root cause applies there.

Not refuted. The await gap is real and the claim's mechanism checks out in code.

Path: bus.server.ts:274 runs desktopGrantConsume (synchronous, hashes checked via manager.server.ts:2171-2183 and authorization.server.ts:249-268). Nothing is awaited between it and found.adapter.execute at bus.server.ts:292. TerminalCapability.execute (local.server.ts:165) calls runProcess with owned:true. On win32, process.server.ts:65 routes that to runWindowsOwnedProcess. That function awaits outputPipe for stdout (owned-process-group.server.ts:137) and again for stderr (line 140) before the OwnedProcessGroup spawn at line 142. node itself is not marked owned, but the owned flag comes from the options, so the Windows owned path is taken. The window therefore covers two named-pipe listens, the native launch, and node's bootstrap before it reads the entry file.

No recheck closes it. The non-agentic grant path has no snapshot: agenticAdmit returns {} when there is no agentic record (manager.server.ts:121-122), so boundedEnvironment and boundedScriptHash are unset and the snapshot/hash check in bounded-terminal.server.ts:78 never runs. The mutationSequence check (authorization.server.ts:267) runs only at consume time. The window is also open to remote writes: filesystem.write to a non-config path is not desktop-required (authorization.server.ts:208-212), and the Host event loop can service a device write during the awaits. So a device filesystem.write landing after consume and before node reads the entry file would run unapproved content under the grant. The race is narrow (tens of ms) and a device must time its write from an event, so the likelihood is low, but the outcome is device-driven code execution, which the policy forbids. I would keep it at MEDIUM rather than LOW. The reviewer's recommendation is sound.

Related issue the reviewer did not raise, which I did not verify dynamically: the same post-consume gap applies to imported modules. The grant binds only the named entry file (fileIdentities, authorization.server.ts:220-238). mutationSequence is compared only at consume (authorization.server.ts:267), and the store counter (store.server.ts:149) is never re-read after spawn. A device can therefore overwrite a module the approved script loads lazily (dynamic import or require later in the run, which can be minutes into a 15-minute run) and the modified code executes under the grant without a race. This is a stronger version of the same defect and deserves its own review entry, likely HIGH.

finding.title: Option-form file arguments escape the terminal grant content hash
finding.scenario: fileIdentities drops every argument beginning with '-' before hashing, so a file named inside an option (node --require=./payload.js, --import=./x.mjs, --loader=./x.mjs) is never content-bound. The workstation approves terminal.exec node with args ["--require=./payload.js","-e","1"]; capabilityOperation records files {} and the digest covers only the argument strings. A paired device can answer an ordinary bounded filesystem.write to payload.js (remoteExecutionRefusal returns null for it, so the write is not refused), replacing the file's contents. At use time desktopGrantViolation still returns null, so the single-use grant launches node, which loads and runs the replaced payload. The separate-form '-r ./payload.js' is hashed and correctly rejected after the same change, so the gap is specific to the '--opt=value' form. Preconditions: the mission envelope must allow node and a write to that file, and the device must answer the write ask in the grant window (5 min).
finding.evidence: Probe (own temp folder, repo modules imported by absolute URL): capabilityOperation('terminal.exec',{command:'node',args:['--require=./payload.js','-e','1']},dir,null).files => {}; same for ['--import=./payload.js'] => {}; ['-r','./payload.js','-e','1'] => {"./payload.js":"e761df..."}. Grant minted over the first op, payload.js rewritten, desktopGrantViolation(grant, ctx(after)) => null (op digests identical). Separate-form control after rewrite => 'The operation differs from the one authorized on the desktop.' remoteExecutionRefusal('filesystem.write',{path:'payload.js'},'WRITE',dir) => null. Round-1 claim 'terminal grants bind content hashes of named files' is incomplete for this form.
finding.recommendation: Hash every argument that resolves to an existing file, including the value after '=' in '--name=value' options (split on the first '=' and test the value). Alternatively refuse remote-approvable interpreter options that name files, or require an exact argument allowlist for node/npm/npx grants. Add a regression test that rewrites a file named by --require=/--import= and expects desktopGrantViolation to refuse.

finding.title: Local-path device-cookie refusal is bypassable and the proxy-header denylist is incomplete
finding.scenario: authorizeBridge treats a request as workstation (local:true, token:null) when Host is loopback, the TCP peer is loopback, and no header in PROXY_HEADERS or x-forwarded-proto is present. The new device-cookie refusal (line 40) only matches the exact form split(';').trim().startsWith('bunny_device='), while the remote path (line 45) parses the same cookie the same way, so the two paths disagree. Probed: Host localhost:8080 + peer 127.0.0.1 + cookie 'bunny_device =DEVTOKEN' (or a tab before '=') returns {local:true,token:null}; the same cookie on a remote origin returns token:null. Also probed with the exact cookie present plus any of x-forwarded-port, x-forwarded-prefix, x-forwarded-ssl, x-forwarded-server, x-original-forwarded-for, x-url-scheme, front-end-https, x-original-url, x-forwarded-host: all return local:true when the exact cookie is absent (the exact cookie form is refused, as intended). A local:true answer makes hostCall and the events route use the workstation credential. Precondition: an intermediary that rewrites Host to loopback and sends none of the listed headers. The documented Cloudflare-style tunnel adds cf-ray, which is denied, so this is not reachable in that configuration; it is a defense-in-depth gap in the round-1 hardening.

finding.title: A one-time approval survives a Host restart on a failed Mission and runs after Retry
finding.scenario: recover() sweeps only missions in running, verifying, waiting_for_user, ready and planning (line 3911). A failed Mission with a sibling step still in state ready and holding approvedOnce is not swept, so the approval survives the restart. failMission (line 983) cancels children and sets the Mission to failed without clearing approvedOnce on ready siblings, and retry() (line 3628) resets only failed and blocked steps. After a restart, a workstation Retry (envelope still valid) starts the sibling and runs its one-time action with no new ask. Probed by writing the failed-Mission state with approvedOnce directly into the store, then restarting: after Retry the Mission completed, b.txt was written, and no open asks existed. The probe state was synthesized; the reachability of a failMission path that leaves such a sibling is inferred from reading the code, not from a live run. Device impact: none, because recover() revokes remote envelopes and Retry refuses a revoked envelope. The affected authority is workstation-approved, and it violates the restart invariant stated in the same function (a one-time decision waiting to execute may not create authority in the new process).
finding.evidence: Probe output: 'after restart: mission failed | B ready | B approvedOnce {requestId,action:filesystem.write}'; 'after retry: mission completed | B completed | b.txt written: true | open asks: []'. Code: manager.server.ts:3911-3917 (missionsIn list), 983-1000 (failMission), 3628-3660 (retry resets only failed/blocked steps).
finding.recommendation: In recover(), clear approvedOnce on every step of every non-terminal Mission, including failed ones. Clear approvedOnce on all steps when a Mission fails (failMission and containMission). In retry(), clear approvedOnce on every step that becomes ready, blocked or pending, so no old one-time allowance can run.

finding.title: A one-time allowance runs before the revoked-envelope check, so a revoked remote envelope can still run an approved step
finding.scenario: decide() returns allow for context.oneTime at line 324, before the envelope is read and before the revoked-envelope deny at line 331. Only the remote-execution check (line 319) runs first, and it refuses only code and config operations. The endDeviceGrants comment claims that 'the revoked envelope still refuses every further admission' (http.server.ts:869), which is false for one-time steps. Probed: a device-granted envelope (authority remote) with a Mission started and one bounded filesystem.write step carrying a device-approved one-time allowance; the envelope was then revoked in the store without a Mission stop, which is the state the endDeviceGrants catch branch (unstopped++) leaves behind. The step still ran: device.txt was written and the Mission completed. Trigger: a workstation revocation whose Mission stop does not run or does not cancel first (the catch branch), or any future revoke path that does not stop the Mission. The window is narrow because stop normally sets its stopping flag before the envelope is observed, so this is defense in depth against the revocation promise.

finding.recommendation: Check envelope.revokedAt and expiresAt before the oneTime allowance (move the two checks above line 324, or pass the envelope through to the oneTime branch). finding.title: Agent re-consent by a device refuses any filesystem write with a code-execution message
finding.scenario: deviceAgenticRefusal calls remoteExecutionRefusal(manifest.id, {}, manifest.risk) for every capability an Agent permits. With empty params, filesystem.write and filesystem.delete are refused ('has no concrete path'), so a paired device cannot re-consent any Agent whose permitted capabilities include a file write. The refusal text reads 'a paired device cannot authorize command or code execution', which is misleading for a file write. The T9R-F01 policy allows devices to approve bounded ordinary file writes, so this is over-restriction. It fails closed, so it is not a security hole.

finding.title: Agent re-consent refuses every permitted filesystem.write/delete for a device
finding.scenario: deviceAgenticRefusal calls remoteExecutionRefusal(manifest.id, {}, manifest.risk) for each permitted capability. For filesystem.write and filesystem.delete, the empty params fail the "no concrete path" check, so DESKTOP_REQUIRED is returned for any Agent whose permitted capabilities include a file write or delete. Post-restart re-consent of a reviewed bounded-file-write Agent is therefore impossible from a phone. The comment says the check targets bound scripts, interpreters and hook-running Git, and the policy allows bounded ordinary file writes remotely, so this is an unintended over-refusal.
finding.evidence: Probe: remoteExecutionRefusal("filesystem.write", {}, "WRITE") -> "Approval required on Windows Host ... filesystem.write has no concrete path."; with {path:"notes.txt"} and cwd C:/p it returns null. authorization.server.ts line 200 is the source of the refusal.
finding.recommendation: For re-consent, judge write and delete by the Agent's permitted resource roots and the execution-config rule, not by empty params. Or document this as deliberate fail-closed behavior and add a test that pins it.
